newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Congress gears up for electricity debate.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Congress gears up for electricity debate.

text.p: The new Congress and the Clinton administration are gearing up to debate how to force the break up of electric utility monopolies, the last big regulated industry in the United States.
At stake are the future of the utilities and the role of states in controlling power supply rates paid by everyone from homeowners to industry.
While some states, led by California, Massachusetts, Pennsylvania and Rhode Island, have already set dates for allowing consumers to shop for power, others are moving more slowly, if at all.
Lawmakers in Washington are looking to push them all in the same direction.

Ignoring concerns about encroaching on states' rights, Republicans and Democrats introduced bills last year to force states to allow all consumers to shop for power by a specific date, ranging from 1998, as proposed by House Republican Whip Tom DeLay of Texas, to 2010, as proposed by Democratic Sen. Bennett Johnston of Louisiana, now retired.
In contrast, the Clinton administration is leaning against mandating a deadline in a bill it is preparing, according to comments by Deputy Energy Secretary Charles Curtis.
Rep. Dan Schaefer, R-Colorado, chairman of the House energy and power panel, planned to reintroduce his bill with minor changes as soon as possible, his spokeswoman said.
Schaefer's bill, the first detailed proposal offered in the House last year, called for open competition among all power producers in the retail market by the end of 2000.

In the Senate, which last year sought only to repeal the Public Utility Holding Company Act, Republican Sen. Don Nickles of Oklahoma said he planned to weigh in with his own comprehensive utility restructuring bill this year.
Nickles, who heads the Senate energy production and regulation panel, would be likely to hold hearings before writing legislation to deregulate the industry, according to his spokesman.
"He wants to talk to everybody to see what they think can be done to improve competiiton and decrease the cost (of electricity) to all consumers," said spokesman Ernie Schultz.
